[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Kubernetes Ingress: Ingress Controllers and Ingress Resources"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Managing external access to services in a Kubernetes cluster is a fundamental requirement for production applications. While Services (like NodePort and LoadBalancer) can expose applications, they often lack advanced routing capabilities such as SSL/TLS termination, name-based virtual hosting, and path-based routing. This is where Ingress comes into play."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"What is an Ingress Resource?"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"An Ingress is an API object that manages external access to the services in a cluster, typically via HTTP. It acts as a smart router, defining rules for how traffic enters the cluster and how it is mapped to backend Services."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Ingress Resources only define routing rules; they do not actually traffic-shape or proxy requests by themselves."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"An Ingress Controller is required to parse the Ingress Resource and apply the configuration to a reverse proxy."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"What is an Ingress Controller?"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike standard Kubernetes controllers (which are compiled into the kube-controller-manager), Ingress Controllers run as pods inside your cluster. Popular options include NGINX Ingress Controller, Traefik, HAProxy, and Envoy. The controller watches the Kubernetes API server for updates to Ingress resources and reconfigures its underlying routing engine accordingly."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Step-by-Step Implementation Guide"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this tutorial, we will deploy a simple application, create an Ingress Resource, and route traffic using an Ingress Controller (assuming NGINX is installed in your cluster)."},{"order":11,"type":"heading","text":"Step 1: Deploy a Sample Application and Service"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"First, create a deployment running a basic web server and expose it via a ClusterIP service."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: hashicorp/http-echo
        args: ["-text=\"Hello from Kubernetes Ingress!\""]
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5678
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-app-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: web-app
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 5678"},{"order":14,"type":"heading","text":"Step 2: Create the Ingress Resource"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Next, define the Ingress resource to route incoming traffic matching the host 'example.local' to our 'web-app-service'."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web-app-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  rules:
  - host: example.local
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: web-app-service
            port:
              number: 80"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Verifying the Setup"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can verify that your Ingress resource was created successfully by running the following kubectl command:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"kubectl get ingress web-app-ingress"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"To test access, map your Ingress controller's external IP to 'example.local' in your local '/etc/hosts' file, then send an HTTP request using curl:"},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"curl -H "Host: example.local" http://<INGRESS_CONTROLLER_IP>/"}]
